title: Safe Extensions, Inc. v. FAA (2007)
summary: An informal adjudication is arbitrary and capricious unless substantial evidence in the material the agency actually had before it supports its factual judgments, and an employee's bare assertions do not qualify.
notes:
Key line: Judge Tatel: "The difference between this informal adjudication and a formal adjudication on the record is thus not the amount of evidence the agency must provide to support its decision, but where the evidence may be found."

Citation: 509 F.3d 593 (D.C. Cir. 2007).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Safe Extensions, Inc., a manufacturer of adjustable light bases used to hold runway lights in airport pavement. The respondents were the Federal Aviation Administration and its Administrator, Marion C. Blakey. Competing manufacturers made fixed light bases, which the FAA treated differently, and two installers, Olson Industries and Siemens Airfield Solutions, had filed comments objecting to the FAA's draft circular. The petition was heard by Circuit Judges Henderson, Tatel and Kavanaugh, with Judge Tatel writing for the court.
sections.Material Facts: Runway light bases must hold their alignment under landing aircraft and snow plows and must be adjustable in height as runways are repaved. Safe Extensions makes adjustable products, raised by twisting a threaded extension; competitors make fixed products, raised by stacking extensions. From 1970 to 2005 the FAA required all light bases to pass a torque test conducted after installation in concrete or grout. Advisory Circular 42D in April 2005 limited the test to adjustable products, and Circular 42E in May 2006 required that adjustable products be tested freestanding, before installation. The FAA circulated a draft 42F to selected companies, received two critical comments, prepared a one page comment resolution asserting that fixed products have inherent anti rotational features and that adjustable bonds had failed in the field, and issued the final 42F on October 17, 2006 unchanged. Products that fail it cannot be placed on the approved list from which airports must buy.
sections.Procedural History: Safe Extensions petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of Advisory Circular 42F on December 15, 2006 under 49 U.S.C. 46110(a), which allows a person with a substantial interest in an FAA order to seek review in that court. The FAA argued that the court lacked jurisdiction because the circular was not an order, because the company lacked prudential standing, because the matter was committed to agency discretion, and, at the court's prompting, because the petition was untimely since the differential treatment began with Circular 42E more than sixty days earlier. After oral argument on October 19, 2007 the court ordered affidavits on the timeliness dispute. It decided the case on December 11, 2007, rejecting every jurisdictional objection and granting the petition on the merits.
sections.Issue: The threshold questions were whether an advisory circular that keeps a product off the FAA approved list is a final order reviewable under section 46110, whether reviewability depends on the agency having compiled an adequate record, and whether the petition was timely. The merits question was whether the FAA acted arbitrarily and capriciously by requiring a freestanding torque test for adjustable products but no torque test at all for fixed products. That raised the question the course cares about: when an agency acts through informal adjudication without notice and comment or a hearing, must its factual judgments still be supported by substantial evidence, and where may a court look for that evidence.
sections.Holding: The court held that the circular was a final order because it determined legal consequences by barring airports from buying nonconforming products, that finality alone triggers section 46110 and the absence of a record is not a jurisdictional bar but a reason to remand, that Safe Extensions had a substantial interest and prudential standing, that the statutory standard of what is necessary for safety is judicially manageable, and that reasonable grounds excused the late filing because the FAA had told industry that 42E would be replaced. On the merits it held the differential treatment arbitrary and capricious. None of the FAA's three rationales was supported by substantial evidence: the claim of longer experience with fixed products had no support, the claim about anti rotational features rested on one employee's unsupported assertion, and the claim of field failures was contradicted by the only comments in the record.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Tatel wrote that the FAA's jurisdictional arguments were wholly meritless. An order under section 46110 need only mark the consummation of the agency's process and determine rights or give rise to legal consequences, and a circular that excludes a product from the approved list plainly does. The FAA's reliance on Deutsche Lufthansa for a record requirement misread a case about whether review was available without a quasi judicial hearing, a question the circuit had since resolved by abandoning the United Gas rule. Florida Power & Light v. Lorion confirmed that an inadequate record calls for remand, not dismissal, and making reviewability depend on a compiled record would let agencies escape review by keeping none. On the merits the court applied Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Board of Governors. Advisory circulars are informal adjudications, so no statute requires notice and comment or a hearing, but the decision must still rest on substantial evidence because a nonarbitrary factual judgment cannot rest on evidence that is not substantial. The difference between formal and informal adjudication is not how much evidence is required but where it may be found. The FAA admitted its appendix contained everything it relied on, and that appendix held only an employee's assertions, which under McDonnell Douglas and Algonquin Gas do not amount to substantial evidence.

topics.lrs-n-substantial-evidence: The FAA’s informal action still needed evidence supporting its distinction between competing products.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The court required record support for an informal adjudication under arbitrary-and-capricious review, applying the same reasoned-decisionmaking demand as hard-look review of rules.
topics.lrs-o-adjudication-stages: The FAA action was classified as informal adjudication, which determined the standard and record the court reviewed.

learning.why: The course uses it to show ADAPSO at work: arbitrary and capricious review of informal action still demands substantial factual support, and finality rather than a compiled record is what makes agency action reviewable.
